en: Now let's talk security, because that
matters. Because you're working with an
agent that can write files, that can delete
files.
And of course, you wanna make sure that it
doesn't erase your hard drive, but you also
wanna make sure it doesn't write a script
that exfiltrates data from your machine, for
example. So security matters. That's why
Codex has multiple security-related
mechanisms and features. For example, that
by default, it all runs in a sandboxed
environment.
No matter how you're using Codex, if you're
working in a project, it can only edit files
in that project. It can't touch anything
else on your system or hard drive. So it has
limited file access. In addition, approvals
are required for certain actions. For
example, if I were using Git, which I am
here, I ran git init,
I could ask it to stage all uncommitted
files and commit with a message of initial
commit. And that actually would trigger a
permission popup like this where it is not
able to run git add right away because this
is one of those commands where OpenAI in the
end decided that they should not be allowed
by default and I have to explicitly permit
this action.
I could also tell it to never ask again for
git add commands Or of course, I could
deny this action and have it not do that,
which is what I'll do here.
So you will see approval popups like this
from time to time for certain actions.
In addition, by default in that sandbox
mode, there is limited network access. So
it's not able to reach out to all kinds of
websites. Instead, it will also ask for
that. And it only has limited web search
access because indeed Codex does have a
built-in web search service or it's using
the web search service by
OpenAI, but that is limited by default and
only provides results that have been parsed
and cached by OpenAI
to avoid that Codex ends up on sites that
may have malicious content like prompts
those sites want to inject into your
sessions.
And these are therefore some sensible
security defaults that aim to help you keep
your environment and your project secure.
Obviously, it will be your job to make the
right decisions when asked for permissions
and to tweak these settings as needed, which
is what we'll explore next.
